**Motivation** — why organisms act and persist — intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, needs, goals and values, the internalization of regulation, and the difference between autonomous and controlled motives; the empirical counterpart of the philosophy of autonomy under `agency` (ADR-023).

| [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) | Expected tangible rewards for merely engaging in an interesting task lower later free-choice engagement with it | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). By their study-by-study account, Cameron and Pierce's rival analysis found the same for this contingency (performance-independent rewards, −0.29), while disputing nearly everything else. Proposed because the rival side is unread here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-047](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-047.md) | A regulation taken in under controlling conditions is introjected rather than integrated, so the social history of how a value was acquired fixes how autonomous acting on it is | Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) and Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)): supports for relatedness and competence are enough to get a value internalized, but only as an introject or a compartmentalized identification; integration also needs autonomy support. The experimental evidence is Deci et al. (1994), as reported: the same amount of internalized behaviour correlated positively with felt freedom and enjoyment under autonomy support and negatively under control. Field studies on parenting, religion and medical training agree, correlationally. This is a historical condition on autonomy of the kind [THEORY-040](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-040.md) asks about, with empirical support, but it has not been tested against matched present endorsement or applied to manipulation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-049.md) | Whether an external event lowers or raises intrinsic motivation depends on whether it is experienced as controlling or as information about competence | Cognitive evaluation theory, as tested by Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)) and summarized by Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)): rewards, feedback, deadlines and choice affect intrinsic motivation through their "functional significance". Controlling events shift the perceived locus of causality outward and undermine it; informational ones affirm competence and enhance it, but only with a sense of autonomy. The meta-analytic pattern fits, and controlling versus informational positive feedback differ by d = −0.78 in four studies. Mediation by felt control is untested for rewards. A behavioural and social-cognitive rival exists and is unread here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-052](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-052.md) | Frustration of the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness is a transdiagnostic process in psychopathology | Vansteenkiste, Ryan and Soenens (2020, [LIT-561](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-561.md)) propose that need frustration, distinct from mere lack of satisfaction, plays "a transdiagnostic role", citing a longitudinal study in which it predicted adolescents' depressive and eating symptoms and "largely accounted for their co-occurrence". Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) had located the etiology of "various forms of psychopathology" in developmental need deprivation, with need substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns as the route. The evidence is correlational, mostly self-report, and from the theory's authors. A partner of the inflexibility account, not a rival. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-054](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-054.md) | A regulation is autonomous to the degree it is integrated with the person's other values and needs: autonomy is graded, and is not set by the order of the attitude that endorses it | Self-determination theory orders motives on a continuum from external through introjected and identified to integrated regulation and intrinsic motivation. Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) place autonomy in integration, "congruence with one's other values and needs", and report a quasi-simplex structure and an experiment in which integrated and introjected internalization behave differently. Ryan and Deci ([LIT-560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-560.md)) align this with hierarchical accounts but grade it. It is the empirical counterpart of [THEORY-029](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-029.md)'s negative claim. It is not shown that integration can be measured apart from endorsement, and it does not escape Velleman's dilemma. | Proposed |
